facts.statement: Sarcoprion is an extinct genus of cartilaginous fish that lived during the Late Permian in Greenland.
facts.quote: Sarcoprion (from the Ancient Greek, "flesh saw") is an extinct genus of cartilaginous fish from the Late Permian of Greenland.

facts.statement: Sarcoprion had an arching row of connected teeth called a tooth whorl in its jaws, along with flattened rectangular teeth in other parts of its mouth.
facts.quote: It possessed an arching row of connected teeth, termed a tooth whorl, in its upper and lower jaws, as well as flattened, rectangular teeth elsewhere in the mouth.

facts.statement: The first four fossils of Sarcoprion edax were discovered in the 1930s by Eigil Nielsen in the Foldvik Creek Formation of East Greenland.
facts.quote: The first four Sarcoprion edax fossils were first discovered during the 1930s by paleontologist Eigil Nielsen, and originated inside concretions from the Foldvik Creek Formation of East Greenland.

facts.statement: The most complete Sarcoprion specimen has a skull and lower jaws nearly 90 cm long, with the total animal length estimated at up to 6 meters by John A. Long.
facts.quote: The most complete known Sarcoprion specimen consists of a skull and lower jaws which are nearly 90 cm long, and the total length of the animal was estimated to be up to 6 m by paleontologist John A. Long.

facts.statement: Eigil Nielsen hypothesized that Sarcoprion was likely unable to close its mouth based on skull and jaw reconstructions.
facts.quote: Nielsen suggested that, based on his reconstruction of the genus' skull and lower jaw, Sarcoprion was likely incapable of closing its mouth.

facts.statement: Nielsen suggested that rows of flattened pavement teeth along the mouth's lateral surfaces likely served as armor for the snout rather than for feeding.
facts.quote: Rows of tile-like, flattened teeth (termed pavement teeth) were present along the lateral surfaces of the mouth in addition to the midline tooth whorls, and Nielsen thought these were likely armor for the snout rather than useful for feeding.

facts.statement: Nielsen, Oleg Lebedev, and Wayne Itano have hypothesized that Sarcoprion used its tooth whorls like scissors to cut prey.
facts.quote: Nielsen, as well as later authors such as Oleg Lebedev and Wayne Itano, have hypothesized that the animal used its whorls like a pair of scissors to cut prey during feeding.

facts.statement: Oleg Lebedev proposed in 2009 that Sarcoprion ate fish and cephalopods, comparing its features to living toothed whales like sperm whales.
facts.quote: In a 2009 paper, Lebedev proposed that features of Sarcoprion's teeth and snout suggest a diet of fish and cephalopods, based on comparisons with living toothed whales such as sperm whales.

facts.statement: John Long speculated that Sarcoprion had a generalist diet including other cartilaginous fish and hard-shelled cephalopods.
facts.quote: John Long has speculated that Sarcoprion had a generalist diet that included other cartilaginous fish as well as hard-shelled cephalopods.

facts.statement: Sarcoprion is classified in the order Eugeneodontiformes and the subclass Holocephali.
facts.quote: It is a member of order Eugeneodontiformes and the larger subclass Holocephali.

facts.statement: Sarcoprion belongs to the family Helicoprionidae.
facts.quote: Sarcoprion is a member of the order Eugeneodontiformes and the family Helicoprionidae.

facts.statement: Sarcoprion is classified within the class Chondrichthyes.
Some sources classify Sarcoprion in the family Agassizodontidae.
The Paleobi Database lists the parent group of Sarcoprion as Helicoprionidae.
The name Sarcoprion comes from Greek roots meaning "flesh" and "saw".
facts.quote: The genus name is derived from the Greek roots sarcos, meaning "flesh", and prion, meaning "saw".

facts.statement: It is debated whether Sarcoprion is related to other eugeneodonts, though earlier hypotheses placing it in a separate group are no longer supported.
facts.quote: Earlier research by paleontologist Svend Erik Bendix-Almgreen suggested that the genus may be unrelated to other fish now called eugeneodonts, and instead be part of a group containing only Erikodus and Fadenia. This is no longer supported.

rejected.statement: Fossils of Sarcoprion lack evidence of a distinct upper jaw, suggesting it may have been fused to the skull, reduced, or lost.
rejected.quote: The known fossils do not show evidence of a distinct upper jaw, implying it may have been fused to the skull, reduced, or lost entirely.
